title: Henrietta Szold founded Hadassah, which brought medicine to the inhabitants of the Land of Israel of all origins and religions

trailer.text: Henrietta Szold, a Jewish American, led Hadassah in its early years, and from 1933 also ran Youth Aliyah.
In 1909 she visited the Land of Israel and was appalled by the poverty and disease among Muslims, Christians and Jews.
On February 24, 1912, she was elected president of Hadassah, which was founded in a synagogue in New York and chose nursing as its focus.
In 1913 Hadassah sent two nurses to Jerusalem, and in 1918 a medical unit set out with 45 doctors and nurses.
From this grew a medical organization that served people of all origins and religions, and according to Time, infant mortality fell from 140 per thousand in 1918 to 29 per thousand by 1948.

stations.title: 1909: What Szold saw in the Land of Israel

paragraphs.text: In 1909 Szold traveled with her mother to the Land of Israel for the first time.
They visited agricultural settlements and holy sites.
According to Hadassah, Szold saw Jews living in camps without proper plumbing and sanitation.
She and her mother were appalled by the poverty and disease among Muslim, Christian and Jewish inhabitants.
Szold was determined to create her own organization, in which women could lead practical social service work.
On February 24, 1912, women gathered at Temple Emanu-El in New York to create a new organization.
They founded the Hadassah Chapter of Daughters of Zion and elected Szold president.
The field they chose to focus on was nursing.
According to one source, from an initial roster of 38 women, the organization grew to 21,000 members in 34 chapters within its first five years.
Hadassah's first major project was an American-style visiting nurse system in Jerusalem, in 1913.
The two nurses sailed on January 18.
According to Hadassah, they were sent to provide pasteurized milk to infants and new mothers, and to eradicate trachoma.
In their first year the nurses saw 5000 patients.
World War I and Turkish repression forced Hadassah to close its nurses' house in 1915.

stations.title: 1918: A medical unit against the epidemics

paragraphs.text: Five years after the nurses, Hadassah organized the American Zionist Medical Unit and helped fund it.
The unit set out in 1918 with 45 doctors and nurses and four hundred tons of supplies.
It brought a field hospital to the Land of Israel, and established hospitals in six cities.
According to Time, at the time of Szold's visit to the Land of Israel in 1909, before Hadassah was founded, there were only twelve doctors in Jerusalem, and only 45 in the whole country.
In the summer of 1918 the unit found successive epidemics in Jerusalem: malaria, typhus, influenza, cholera, dysentery and the Black Death.
The British general Allenby sent a Hadassah team to Tiberias, and the team found cholera rampant there.
According to an article at Ben-Gurion University, officially the unit did not belong to Hadassah, but the people of the Yishuv called it Hadassah.
Szold herself was a pacifist, and therefore at first could not enter the Land of Israel.
According to the encyclopedia Encyclopedia.com, Henrietta Szold moved to the Land of Israel in 1920 and began overseeing the daily activity of Hadassah projects.

stations.title: Medicine for all origins and religions

paragraphs.text: Szold envisioned an American standard of medicine for all inhabitants of the Land of Israel, regardless of race, religion or nationality.
She transformed the emergency effort into the "Hadassah Medical Organization".
The organization emphasized the needs of women and children and served people of all origins and religions.
She and her colleagues shaped an institution in which treatment was provided without consideration of race, nationality or religion.
Under her leadership, Hadassah became the largest and most powerful Zionist organization in the United States.
The organization raised funds and set up hospitals, food banks, nursing schools and social programs.
Hadassah created the infrastructure for a modern medical system that would serve both Jews and Arabs.
According to Time, infant mortality fell from 140 per thousand in 1918 to 29 per thousand by 1948.
According to Time, trachoma among schoolchildren fell from 34% to 4.3%, and ringworm from 40% to 1%.

According to an article written for Hadassah's centennial, the Hadassah Medical Organization was then centered in Jerusalem, and it included two hospitals and related institutions that employed more than 5,000 people.
According to an article written for Hadassah's centennial, Arab doctors, janitors, nurses and laboratory technicians then made up about 20 percent of the medical center's staff.
According to the writer in Dissent, in the past very few non-Jewish workers and only a handful of Arab patients were seen at the hospital.
In 1933, as the situation of Jews in Germany deteriorated, Szold ran Youth Aliyah.
She tried to meet every arriving transport of children.
She gave personal attention to the placement and situation of every child.
Szold was not the first to conceive of Youth Aliyah as a rescue of young people from Nazi Europe.
In 1936 The Nation chose her as one of the important Americans.
Szold died in Jerusalem on February 13, 1945, at the modern medical center that Hadassah had built.
Thousands attended her funeral, and a boy from Youth Aliyah said Kaddish.
In 1949 Hadassah inaugurated the Henrietta Szold Prize, and that year it was awarded to Eleanor Roosevelt.
Kibbutz Kfar Szold in the Upper Galilee is named after her.
In 2005 the Hadassah Medical Organization was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, for advanced medical care for all regardless of race, origin or nationality.
According to the encyclopedia, Szold insisted on American standards and work habits, and this met with stout resistance.
Labor circles saw this as medical imperialism.
Leaders of the Federation of American Zionists criticized Hadassah for not engaging in Zionist work designed to turn the Jews into a political entity.
When the Hebrew University was founded, Szold was not given a seat on the board because she was a woman.
In 1942 Szold was one of the founders of Ihud, a party in the Land of Israel that sought a binational solution.
The party was willing to limit Jewish immigration even during the extermination of European Jews, and remained marginal.
Szold's support for a binational state and her membership in Brit Shalom brought her much criticism from within Zionist circles, and also from within Hadassah.
On April 13, 1948, Arabs from nearby villages attacked a convoy to the hospital on Mount Scopus, killing seventy-nine people.

claims.text: לפי JWA, הגיל בין סאלד לגינצברג היה שלוש עשרה שנים והיא המבוגרת.
claims.quote: Szold had long accepted that the difference in their ages (she was thirteen years his senior) precluded any realistic hope of romantic attachment.

claims.text: לפי ויקיפדיה, גינצברג היה צעיר ממנה בחמש עשרה שנים והחזיר את רגשותיה רק באופן אפלטוני.
claims.quote: He was fifteen years her junior, and he returned her feelings only platonically.

claims.text: לפי האנציקלופדיה Encyclopedia.com, הנרייטה סאלד עברה לארץ ישראל ב-1920 והחלה לפקח על הפעילות היומיומית של פרויקטי הדסה.
claims.quote: Henrietta Szold finally moved to Palestine in 1920 and began overseeing the daily operation of Hadassah projects.
